\chapter{The Welded Teens}
\label{ch:numbers-11-16}
\hlchaptermodality{14}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count from eleven to sixteen in French, and say which half of each word is the digit and which is the ten.}

Six numbers French did not build. It inherited them from Latin already welded shut — ūndecim, duodecim, trēdecim — and wore them down to one syllable each. The -ze they all share is decem, the same ten already hiding in dix and in décembre, and the front of every one of them is its own digit: deux in douze, six in seize. The digit comes first and the ten comes second, which is a choice, and French is about to make the other one.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[onze]{onze — eleven}

\label{lesson:FR-C12-onze}



\begin{quote}
You can count to ten. The eleventh number is where you find out that French did not build its teens at all — it inherited them, already welded shut.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{nasal-on} — the \textbf{on} is a \textbf{nasal vowel}, the same one you have in \textbf{bonjour}.
  \item \texttt{z-voiced} — the \textbf{z} is buzzed, not hissed: your throat should vibrate.
  \item Together: \textbf{onze} = \emph{ONZ}, one syllable.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{onze} is Latin \textbf{ūndecim} — \emph{ūnus} (\textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{}) plus \emph{decem} (\textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{}), fused into one word before French existed.

Notice what French did \textbf{not} do. English says \emph{eleven}, which is its own strange word; German says \emph{elf}. French could have said \textbf{dix-un}, \textquotedblleft{}ten-one,\textquotedblright{} and it does not. It took the Latin compound whole and wore it down: \emph{ūndecim} $\to$ \emph{onze}, four syllables into one.

That is worth flagging now, because it will not last. French keeps this inherited style for exactly six numbers, and then abandons it in front of you.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}onze\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ONZ}, the vowel through the nose, the \emph{z} buzzed
  \item the count so far — \textquotedblleft{}huit, neuf, dix, onze\textquotedblright{}
  \item what is inside it — \textquotedblleft{}ūnus plus decem: one-ten\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say eleven? (\textbf{onze}, \emph{ONZ}.) What two Latin words are fused inside it? (\emph{\textbf{ūnus}} and \emph{\textbf{decem}} — \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{}.) Did French build this word out of \emph{dix} and \emph{un}? (\textbf{No} — it inherited \emph{ūndecim} already joined.) Next: twelve, the same way.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[douze]{douze — twelve}

\label{lesson:FR-C12-douze}



\begin{quote}
One welded number could be an accident. Two of them is a pattern, and this one lets you hear the join.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-ou} — \textbf{ou} is a single pure \textbf{oo}, as in English \emph{food}. Never two sounds.
  \item \texttt{z-voiced} — the same buzzed \textbf{z} as \textbf{onze}.
  \item Together: \textbf{douze} = \emph{DOOZ}, one syllable.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{douze} is Latin \textbf{duodecim} — \emph{duo} (\textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{}) plus \emph{decem} (\textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{}).

And this time you can see both halves survive into the French. Say \textbf{deux}, then say \textbf{douze}, and listen to the front of each: \emph{deu-}, \emph{dou-}. That is the same digit, and it did not disappear — it was only worn down.

The back half is doing the same thing. \textbf{onze} and \textbf{douze} both end in \textbf{-ze}, and both come from a Latin word ending in \emph{-decim}. Two words, one shared ending, and a strong hint about where that ending came from.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}douze\textquotedblright{} — \emph{DOOZ}, the \emph{ou} a single pure vowel
  \item the digit surfacing — \textquotedblleft{}deux, douze\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}onze, douze\textquotedblright{}; hear the shared ending
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say twelve? (\textbf{douze}, \emph{DOOZ}.) Which small number can you hear at the front of it? (\emph{\textbf{deux}}.) What Latin word is it from? (\emph{\textbf{duodecim}}.) What ending do \emph{onze} and \emph{douze} share? (\textbf{-ze}.) Next: what that \textbf{-ze} actually is.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-ze]{-ze — the ten you keep meeting}

\label{lesson:FR-C12-ze-decem}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Onze} and \emph{douze} share an ending. Before you learn four more words that also share it, it is worth two minutes to find out what it \textbf{is} — because you have already met it twice, wearing other clothes.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
The \textbf{-ze} on the end of \emph{onze} and \emph{douze} is Latin \textbf{decem}, \textquotedblleft{}ten.\textquotedblright{}

That is all it is. \emph{ūn-decim} $\to$ \emph{on-ze}. \emph{duo-decim} $\to$ \emph{dou-ze}. The Latin \emph{-decim} has been ground down to a single buzzed consonant and a silent vowel, but it is still the word \textbf{ten}, still sitting in the back half of the number, still telling you what the number is built on.

Now put it beside the other two places you have already met that same \emph{decem}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{dix} — ten itself, worn down from \emph{decem} at the front instead of the back
  \item \textbf{décembre} — the old \textbf{tenth} month, which kept \emph{decem} almost intact
  \item \textbf{-ze} — the same ten, welded onto a digit and nearly erased
\end{itemize}

One Latin root, three disguises, and you now hold all three. This is the single most useful habit this book can give you: when a scrap of a word looks familiar, it usually is, and the long word is the one that tells you what the short one was.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three disguises — \textquotedblleft{}dix, décembre, onze\textquotedblright{}
  \item the claim — \textquotedblleft{}the -ze is decem; it means ten\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two you have — \textquotedblleft{}onze, douze\textquotedblright{}; and hear the ten on the end of both
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the \textbf{-ze} of \emph{onze} and \emph{douze}? (Latin \textbf{decem}, \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{}.) Name two other French words where you have already met that same \emph{decem}. (\textbf{dix} and \textbf{décembre}.) Which of the three kept it most intact? (\textbf{décembre}.) Next: thirteen, with the ten now visible on the end.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[treize]{treize — thirteen}

\label{lesson:FR-C12-treize}



\begin{quote}
With the \textbf{-ze} identified, the rest of the welded teens stop being words to memorise and start being sums you can read.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item The \textbf{ei} is the open \textbf{è} you met in \emph{père} and \emph{frère} — \emph{treh}, not \emph{tray}.
  \item \texttt{z-voiced} — the buzzed \textbf{z} again.
  \item Together: \textbf{treize} = \emph{TREHZ}, one syllable, with the throat \textbf{r} at the front.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{treize} is Latin \textbf{trēdecim} — \emph{trēs} (\textquotedblleft{}three\textquotedblright{}) plus \emph{decem} (\textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{}).

Read it as a sum now rather than a word:

\textbf{trei-} is \emph{trois}, worn down · \textbf{-ze} is \emph{decem}, worn down

Say \textbf{trois}, then \textbf{treize}, and the front half answers for itself. You are not learning a thirteenth arbitrary noise; you are reading \emph{three} and \emph{ten} stuck together and then rubbed smooth.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}treize\textquotedblright{} — \emph{TREHZ}, the open \emph{è}
  \item the digit surfacing — \textquotedblleft{}trois, treize\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three you have — \textquotedblleft{}onze, douze, treize\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say thirteen? (\textbf{treize}, \emph{TREHZ}.) What are its two halves? (\emph{\textbf{trois}} and the \textbf{-ze} that is \textbf{decem}.) Count from eleven. (\emph{Onze, douze, treize}.) Next: fourteen, the longest of them.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[quatorze]{quatorze — fourteen}

\label{lesson:FR-C12-quatorze}



\begin{quote}
Every teen so far has been one syllable. This one is two, and the reason is that it started out longer than any of them.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{quatorze} = \emph{ka-TORZ}. Two syllables, weight on the second.
  \item The \textbf{qu} is a plain \textbf{k}, exactly as in \textbf{quatre} — never a \emph{kw}.
  \item \texttt{z-voiced} — the buzzed \textbf{z} closes it, like all the others.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{quatorze} is Latin \textbf{quattuordecim} — \emph{quattuor} (\textquotedblleft{}four\textquotedblright{}) plus \emph{decem}.

\emph{Quattuordecim} is five syllables. \emph{Quatorze} is two. French has thrown away more than half the word and still kept both ideas: \textbf{quator-} is the four, \textbf{-ze} is the ten.

Set it beside its own digit — \textbf{quatre}, \emph{KATR} — and the family resemblance is obvious once you stop expecting the spelling to match. Both begin \emph{quat-}; the number simply grew a syllable to carry the ten.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}quatorze\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ka-TORZ}, the \emph{qu} a plain \emph{k}
  \item the digit surfacing — \textquotedblleft{}quatre, quatorze\textquotedblright{}
  \item the four you have — \textquotedblleft{}onze, douze, treize, quatorze\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say fourteen? (\textbf{quatorze}, \emph{ka-TORZ}.) How is the \textbf{qu} pronounced? (A plain \textbf{k}.) What Latin word is behind it? (\emph{\textbf{quattuordecim}}.) Count from eleven. (\emph{Onze, douze, treize, quatorze}.) Next: fifteen.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[quinze]{quinze — fifteen}

\label{lesson:FR-C12-quinze}



\begin{quote}
Back to one syllable — and this is the teen whose Latin half you are most likely to already know from English.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{nasal-in} — the \textbf{in} is the nasal vowel you have in \textbf{pain} and \textbf{vin}.
  \item The \textbf{qu} is a plain \textbf{k} again.
  \item Together: \textbf{quinze} = \emph{KANZ}, one syllable, the vowel through the nose.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{quinze} is Latin \textbf{quīndecim} — \emph{quīnque} (\textquotedblleft{}five\textquotedblright{}) plus \emph{decem}.

The French digit \textbf{cinq} has travelled a long way from \emph{quīnque}, so \emph{quinze} does not obviously look like \emph{cinq}. But the Latin \textbf{quīn-} is loud in English, and that is the way in:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{quin}tet — a group of five
  \item \textbf{quin}tuplet — one of five
  \item \textbf{quin}tessence — the \emph{fifth} essence, the one the ancients added to earth, water, air and fire
\end{itemize}

So when \emph{cinq} and \emph{quinze} refuse to look related, go through English: \emph{quintet} is the bridge between them.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}quinze\textquotedblright{} — \emph{KANZ}, the vowel through the nose
  \item the bridge — \textquotedblleft{}cinq, quintet, quinze\textquotedblright{}
  \item the five you have — \textquotedblleft{}onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say fifteen? (\textbf{quinze}, \emph{KANZ}.) Which English words carry the same \emph{quīn-}? (\textbf{quintet}, \textbf{quintuplet}, \textbf{quintessence}.) Why is that useful here? (\emph{cinq} and \emph{quinze} \textbf{do not look alike}; the English word is the \textbf{bridge} between them.) Next: sixteen, the last of the welded ones.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[seize]{seize — sixteen}

\label{lesson:FR-C12-seize}



\begin{quote}
The sixth and last of them. After this word the pattern you have spent five lessons learning simply stops — which is the next chapter's whole subject.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item The \textbf{ei} is the open \textbf{è}, the same vowel as \textbf{treize}.
  \item \texttt{z-voiced} — the buzzed \textbf{z} one last time.
  \item Together: \textbf{seize} = \emph{SEHZ}. Say \textbf{treize} and \textbf{seize} back to back: one consonant apart, and they rhyme exactly.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{seize} is Latin \textbf{sēdecim} — \emph{sex} (\textquotedblleft{}six\textquotedblright{}) plus \emph{decem}.

That is the sixth and final inherited compound. Latin had them beyond this point too, but French did not keep them, and you are about to see what it did instead.

Note also what \textbf{seize} is not. It is \textbf{not} \emph{dix-six}. Nothing in the first six teens is built out of \emph{dix} plus a digit — every one of them arrived from Latin already joined, and French merely wore them down. That distinction is the thing to hold on to going into the next chapter.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}seize\textquotedblright{} — \emph{SEHZ}
  \item the rhyme — \textquotedblleft{}treize, seize\textquotedblright{}
  \item all six — \textquotedblleft{}onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say sixteen? (\textbf{seize}, \emph{SEHZ}.) Which other teen rhymes with it? (\textbf{treize}.) Is it built from \emph{dix} and \emph{six}? (\textbf{No} — it came from Latin \emph{sēdecim} already \textbf{fused}.) Count all six. (\emph{Onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize}.) Next: which end of each word is the digit.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[trei-ze]{trei-\textbf{ze} — which half is which}

\label{lesson:FR-C12-digit-first}



\begin{quote}
You have six words and you know their ending is \emph{ten}. One question is left, and it is the one that makes the next chapter make sense: \textbf{which end of the word is the digit?}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: digit in front, ten behind}]
In all six, the \textbf{digit comes first} and the \textbf{ten comes second}. \emph{Trēdecim} is \textquotedblleft{}three-ten,\textquotedblright{} \textbf{not} \textquotedblleft{}ten-three.\textquotedblright{}

Each word is its own small number worn down, with the ten stuck on the back:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{number} & \textbf{the digit in front} & \textbf{the ten behind} \\
\midrule
onze & \textbf{on-} $\leftarrow$ \emph{un} & \textbf{-ze} \\
douze & \textbf{dou-} $\leftarrow$ \emph{deux} & \textbf{-ze} \\
treize & \textbf{trei-} $\leftarrow$ \emph{trois} & \textbf{-ze} \\
quatorze & \textbf{quator-} $\leftarrow$ \emph{quatre} & \textbf{-ze} \\
quinze & \textbf{quin-} $\leftarrow$ \emph{cinq} & \textbf{-ze} \\
seize & \textbf{sei-} $\leftarrow$ \emph{six} & \textbf{-ze} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say each pair slowly — \emph{deux, douze}; \emph{six, seize} — and the small number surfaces every time.

Hold on to the \textbf{order}, not just the halves. Digit-first is a choice, and a language can make the other one. French is about to.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the rule — \textquotedblleft{}digit first, ten second\textquotedblright{}
  \item the six pairs — \textquotedblleft{}un/onze, deux/douze, trois/treize, quatre/quatorze, cinq/quinze, six/seize\textquotedblright{}
  \item the shape of one — \textquotedblleft{}trei- is three, -ze is ten\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
In \emph{treize}, which half is the three and which is the ten? (\textbf{trei-} is the three; \textbf{-ze} is the ten.) So is 13 built as \textquotedblleft{}three-ten\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}ten-three\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Three-ten} — the \textbf{digit comes first}.) Which digit is hiding in \emph{quatorze}? (\emph{\textbf{quatre}}.) Next chapter: the number where French reverses that order and stops fusing altogether.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — eleven to sixteen}

\label{lesson:FR-C12-practice-teens}



\begin{quote}
Six words, learned one at a time. Run them as a block, then take each one apart again from memory.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: the run}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize\textquotedblright{}
  \item from ten — \textquotedblleft{}dix, onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize\textquotedblright{}
  \item backwards — \textquotedblleft{}seize, quinze, quatorze, treize, douze, onze\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{Your turn: surface the digit}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item each pair — \textquotedblleft{}un/onze, deux/douze, trois/treize\textquotedblright{}
  \item the harder three — \textquotedblleft{}quatre/quatorze, cinq/quinze, six/seize\textquotedblright{}
  \item the one that needs English — \textquotedblleft{}cinq, quintet, quinze\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the ten on the end}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three disguises — \textquotedblleft{}dix, décembre, -ze\textquotedblright{}
  \item one sum aloud — \textquotedblleft{}trei- is three, -ze is ten, treize is thirteen\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{six numbers}, eleven to sixteen.
  \item \textbf{one ending explained} — the \textbf{-ze} is \emph{decem}, the same ten you already had in \textbf{dix} and \textbf{décembre}. Three disguises, one root.
  \item \textbf{the order} — digit in front, ten behind. \emph{Treize} is \textquotedblleft{}three-ten.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{a way in when a word refuses} — \emph{cinq} and \emph{quinze} do not look alike, and English \textbf{quintet} stands between them. Reach for the long formal English word whenever the short French one has worn past recognition.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Count eleven to sixteen without stopping. (\emph{Onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize}.) What is the \textbf{-ze}? (Latin \textbf{decem}, \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{}.) Which comes first in these words, the digit or the ten? (The \textbf{digit}.) Which digit is in \emph{quatorze}? (\emph{\textbf{quatre}}.) Were any of these built out of \emph{dix} plus a digit? (\textbf{No} — all six arrived from Latin already \textbf{fused}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
